column6: The commentary makes the front place in a running file a warning that the first arrival need not win; Qohelet explicitly says the race is not won by the swift in its reflection on time and chance.
Hebrew אַחֲרִית, “end/latter,” is a close cognate of the commentary's ء خ ر/آخرة label; Qohelet says a thing's end is better than its beginning, giving the positional sequence a wisdom analogue.

Paul's athletic image has all runners race and tells hearers to run so as to obtain the prize; it gives the commentary's animal race an ethical and eschatological goal without identifying the two scenes.
Paul joins an athlete's self-control to a perishable versus imperishable crown, closely pairing the commentary's run held in reserve with its contrast between what passes and what endures.
Paul forgets what is behind and stretches toward what is ahead while pursuing Christ's prize; this makes the commentary's rear/front positions a deliberate spiritual movement.
In the next step of Paul's race image, he presses toward a goal and an upward prize, supplying an explicit finish-point for the commentary's running sequence.
After teaching about reward, Jesus says that many first will be last and last first; this is a direct eschatological reversal of the commentary's claim that the first to arrive does not thereby win.
Paul's resurrection argument explicitly orders the natural before the spiritual; its later, heavenly mode gives a precise Christian form to the commentary's first/later contrast.

In the sea-escape scene, the divine messenger and cloud move from before Israel's camp to stand behind it, a concrete fore-and-rear file that gives the commentary's spatial sequence theological action.
Isaiah's restoration procession has YHWH go before the people and Israel's God gather their rear; it supplies a second, non-racing use of the commentary's leader-and-tail arrangement.
Against a false prophet, Deuteronomy commands Israel to walk after God; its bodily following turns the commentary's secondary “follow a trace” motion into covenantal allegiance.
Christ's suffering is presented as an example so believers may follow in his steps; the explicit step/track image closely meets the commentary's أثر sense of coming in another's trace.
The heavenly group follows the Lamb wherever he goes and is called firstfruits; its leader, followers, and first portion make it a particularly close eschatological counterpart to the running file.
The wisdom teacher says he has guided the pupil in paths of uprightness, directly joining S87:3's divine guidance with the commentary's image of well-directed movement.
Proverbs promises that the taught person's steps will not be cramped and that running will not cause stumbling; it is a direct ethical counterpart to the animal with a smooth, well-placed gait.
Isaiah says God makes level the path of the righteous; the verse turns the commentary's ease and orderly footfall into a divine smoothing of a human way.
The psalm pictures the sun as a bridegroom and a strong man running his course across the sky, a specific biblical meeting of celestial motion and the commentary's running image.
At creation the morning stars sing together; this gives the commentary's moving stars a scriptural role of cosmic praise rather than merely astronomical motion.
Psalm 148 summons sun, moon, and all shining stars to praise, directly bringing S87:1's praise and the commentary's celestial swimmers into one liturgical scene.
The same psalm calls creatures to praise YHWH's Name because it alone is exalted above earth and heaven, closely matching “the Name of your Lord, the Most High.”
In a royal plea, some invoke chariots and horses while the faithful remember the Name of YHWH; it links the commentary's horse imagery to S87:15's remembrance of the divine Name.
God's questions about the fixed ordinances and rule of the heavens supply a biblical frame for S87:3's measuring and guiding and for the commentary's ordered stellar courses.

1 Clement depicts heaven, day and night, sun, moon, and stars completing their prescribed courses without deviation; it is an unusually close Christian expansion of the commentary's orbital movement under divine determination.
Psalm 47 calls YHWH “Most High” and a great king over all the earth, providing the Hebrew Bible's direct divine title beside S87:1.

The commentary insists that the second-horse resonance of ص ل و does not replace prayer; Biblical Aramaic מְצַלֵּא in Daniel's thrice-daily kneeling is a close cognate and preserves that primary prayer sense.
Jesus' model prayer begins by hallowing the Father's Name, a close liturgical counterpart to remembering the Lord's Name and then praying in S87:15.
In thanksgiving worship the psalmist offers sacrifice and calls on YHWH's Name, a Hebrew Bible pairing of invocation of the Name with prayerful worship.
Isaiah contrasts grass and flower that wither with God's word that stands forever, giving an exact durable-versus-vanishing form to S87:16-17's worldly and abiding contrast.
Daniel's awakening of the dead includes everlasting life and everlasting abhorrence, placing the commentary's “more enduring” latter state in an explicit Jewish eschatological scene.

column5: vestibule before the World to Come
column6: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the World to Come and tells hearers to prepare in it for the banquet hall, making the commentary's near/after sequence into a spatial ethical preparation.

column5: this world and World to Come
column6: Avot says an hour of bliss in the World to Come exceeds all life here, but also that present repentance and good deeds exceed the whole World to Come; it both parallels S87:17 and guards against treating present life as valueless.

column5: today for doing, tomorrow for reward
column6: The rabbinic interpretation, “today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward,” gives the commentary's first/later sequence a disciplined present-work and later-reward reading.

column5: life in this world and eternal life
column6: Jesus says that loving one's life in this world loses it, while relinquishing it here keeps it for eternal life; this is one of the closest New Testament formulations of S87:16-17's contrast.
Paul contrasts visible things that are temporary with unseen things that are eternal, directly articulating the commentary's “near” present and more abiding latter reality.
First John says the world and its desire pass away, while the doer of God's will remains forever; its passing/remain contrast closely tracks the commentary's dunya and أبقى contrast.

column5: no abiding city, city to come
column6: Hebrews says believers have no enduring city here but seek the one to come, using an explicit spatial and durable/future contrast for the commentary's near shore and later destination.
Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people rather than temporary enjoyment of sin, supplying a concrete counterchoice to the preference for immediate worldly life.
Moses treats reproach as greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; it gives the commentary's better latter outcome a stated reason for reordering present preference.

column5: treasure where it is not destroyed
column6: Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven, where moth, corrosion, and thieves do not destroy it; the storing image clarifies what “more enduring” means without making the horse's reserve literal wealth.

In the rich man and Lazarus story, Abraham contrasts the rich man's good things in life with Lazarus's present comfort and the rich man's distress; it narrates the temporal reversal developed in the commentary.

column5: storing for the future and true life
column6: Those rich in this age are told to store a good foundation for the future and take hold of true life, a direct ethical alternative to preferring the immediately available life.
Paul says he has finished the race and kept the faith; this gives the commentary's animal that holds strength toward the end a human image of faithful completion.

The verse's מֵאַחֲרֵיהֶם, “behind them,” is a close Hebrew cognate of the commentary's ء خ ر family; its use is spatial in the cloud scene, so it supports the rear-of-a-file sense without importing an afterlife meaning.
Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light; it offers a Christian ethical use of ease beside S87:8, though it is a yoke rather than the commentary's animal's smooth gait.

column5: swift as a deer to do God's will
column6: Avot tells the reader to be swift as a deer in doing the heavenly Father's will, a Jewish ethical transformation of animal speed that helps frame the commentary's running animals.
Deborah's song portrays stars fighting Sisera from their courses; it offers a biblical use of moving celestial tracks, although it does not describe orbital swimming.

1 Enoch invites attention to the heavenly luminaries that do not depart from their ordered paths, an early Jewish development of measured celestial motion relevant to the commentary's stars and divine guidance.
Daniel thanks and praises God for wisdom and power with מְשַׁבַּח, likely cognate with the commentary's س ب ح label; it supports the praise sense, not the commentary's horse or swimming associations.

column5: tyrant aspiring to the Most High
column6: The Babylonian king says he will make himself like the Most High and is answered by descent in the surrounding oracle; beside the commentary's Pharaoh allusion, it contrasts a false highest lord with praise of the true one.
Esau eats the immediate meal and despises his birthright; while it is not an afterlife text, the narrative supplies a concrete Jewish pattern of preferring what is now over a lasting inheritance.
Those who hope in YHWH run and do not grow weary; it supplies a biblical endurance image beside the commentary's horse that reserves part of its running power.
Avot tells readers to run toward even a light commandment and flee transgression; it makes running a moral direction, though it does not itself contain the worldly/afterlife comparison.

Psalm 147 says that God takes no pleasure in a horse's strength or in human legs; it gives the commentary's running-horse figure a theological counterweight by refusing to make speed or power the ground of success.

column5: God delights in fear and hope
column6: The verse supplies the positive counterpart to the preceding horse image: YHWH delights in those who fear him and hope for his steadfast love, redirecting the running sequence toward trust rather than athletic advantage.
The psalmist says he will run in the way of God's commandments because God enlarges his heart; it makes the commentary's running movement an obedient, enabled course.
Proverbs promises that acknowledging God brings straight paths; its straightened route supplies a concise biblical analogue to S87:3's guidance and the commentary's smooth gait.

column5: led in right paths for the Name
column6: The shepherd restores and leads in paths of righteousness for the sake of his Name, combining the commentary's leader/follower motion with the Name named in S87:15.
YHWH identifies himself as the one who teaches what benefits and leads Israel in the way it should go; it is a particularly close covenantal formulation of “measured, then guided.”
The preparation of YHWH's way levels uneven ground and makes rough places a plain, giving the commentary's easy, well-placed footfall a concrete highway image.
In Isaiah's call to justice, the people's righteousness goes before them and YHWH's glory guards from behind; this ethical procession develops both ends of the commentary's moving line.

column5: stars brought out by number and called by name
column6: Isaiah asks who brings out the heavenly host by number and calls every star by name; it joins the commentary's stars in their courses to divine measuring, ordering, and command.

column5: Mazzaroth in season and Ayish guided
column6: God asks whether a human can bring Mazzaroth out in its season or guide Ayish with its children; this supplies a precise scriptural image of divine guidance of celestial bodies.

column5: statutes of moon and stars, stirred sea
column6: Jeremiah calls the regularity of moon and stars their fixed statutes while also naming the God who stirs the sea; its juxtaposition is a close biblical frame for the commentary's ordered stars and swimming-water imagery.

column5: Most High, Aramaic praise, lives forever
column6: In WLC's Aramaic numbering (often English Dan.4.34), the humbled king blesses the Most High, uses שַׁבְּחֵת for praise, and confesses the one who lives forever; it gathers the commentary's س ب ح, “Most High,” and enduring themes in a reversal of false sovereignty.

The commentary warns that preferring “the life of this world” misorders desire, whereas Deuteronomy commands Israel to choose life as covenant blessing; the contrast matters because the two texts give “life” different ethical functions.

column5: righteous live forever and have reward
column6: Wisdom's final vindication says that the righteous live forever and their reward is with the Lord, a Second Temple Jewish expression of the more abiding latter good.

The martyred brother expects the King of the universe to raise those dying for the law to an eternal renewal of life; its costly present action and enduring future outcome sharpen S87:16-17's comparison.

column5: World to Come without bodily consumption
column6: The rabbinic description of the World to Come removes eating, drinking, and ordinary worldly competition and has the righteous delight in divine radiance; it gives a concrete Jewish interpretation of a superior, lasting future state.

column5: guide our feet into the way of peace
column6: The Benedictus says that the dawn from on high will guide human feet into the way of peace, directly meeting S87:3's guidance and the commentary's attention to ordered footfall.

column5: run with endurance the race set before
column6: Hebrews urges believers to run with endurance the race set before them; the explicit need to last through a course closely complements the commentary's horse that preserves running power for the end.

column5: make straight paths for your feet
column6: Hebrews instructs readers to make straight paths for their feet so that the disabled may be healed rather than turned aside, a Christian ethical use of the commentary's smooth, guided gait.
Jesus says that the one who endures to the end will be saved; it gives the commentary's emphasis on what lasts at the end a direct eschatological criterion.
Hebrews says dispossessed believers know they have a better and abiding possession; its paired comparative is exceptionally close to S87:17's “better and more enduring.”
The patriarchs seek a better country, explicitly identified as heavenly; the verse gives the commentary's distant/later destination a pilgrim-country image.

Jesus tells hearers not to work for food that perishes but for food that endures to eternal life, closely matching the commentary's warning against priority for the immediately available and perishable.
Jesus asks what profits someone who gains the whole world but forfeits life; its whole-world versus life calculation is a sharp Gospel counterpart to preference for dunya.

After comparing bodily training with godliness, the verse says godliness promises both the present life and the coming life; it qualifies the commentary's contrast by valuing present life within a future-oriented discipline.
First Peter describes an inheritance as imperishable, undefiled, unfading, and kept in heaven; its safeguarded future good gives a Christian image for S87:17's abiding outcome.

column5: momentary affliction, eternal weight of glory
column6: Paul says momentary, light affliction produces an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison; its time-scale makes the commentary's near/later reversal explicit.

column5: feet like a hind and high places
column6: Habakkuk says the Lord makes his feet like a hind's and lets him tread high places; it is a divine-strength reading of animal footwork, though not a race or file.
The wicked speakers urge one another to enjoy present good things before they pass; their voice gives a specific Jewish portrayal of the immediate-life preference criticized in the commentary.

column5: two spirits in which to walk
column6: The Community Rule says God assigned humanity spirits of truth and perversity in which to walk until visitation; it develops divine ordering, directed walking, and divergent outcomes without the animal imagery.

column5: works prepared beforehand to walk in
column6: Believers are created for good works that God prepared beforehand so they might walk in them; it offers a Christian formulation of a divinely prepared and guided way.
Hebrews rereads Esau's sale of his birthright for one meal as a warning against irreverence, giving the immediate-versus-lasting choice in Gen.25 a Christian moral interpretation.

Jude calls false teachers wandering stars reserved for deepest darkness; as a moral inversion of the commentary's stars moving in ordered courses, it is image-based rather than an astronomical parallel.

column5: two ways of life and death
column6: The Didache's opening formula distinguishes a way of life from a way of death; it is a Christian two-way framework beside S87:3, 8, and 16-17, though it does not share the running-file scene.
